source_text: Οὐκ ἔχουσιν ἴδιον λόγον, ἔχουσι δὲ τὸν τῆς φύσεως νόμον ἰσχυρῶς ἐνιδρυμένον, καὶ τὸ πρακτέον ὑποδεικνύντα. Βαδίσωμεν, φασὶν, ἐπὶ τὸ βόρειον πέλαγος. Γλυκύτερον γὰρ τῆς λοιπῆς θαλάσσης ἐκεῖνο τὸ ὕδωρ, διότι ἐπ' ὀλίγον αὐτῇ προσδιατρίβων ὁ ἥλιος, οὐκ ἐξάγει αὐτῆς ὅλον διὰ τῆς ἀκτῖνος τὸ πότιμον. Χαίρει δὲ τοῖς γλυκέσι καὶ τὰ θαλάσσια· ὅθεν καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς ποταμοὺς ἀνανήχεται πολλάκις, καὶ πόρρω θαλάσσης φέρεται. Ἐκ τούτου προτιμότερος αὐτοῖς ὁ Πόντος τῶν λοιπῶν ἐστι κόλπων, ὡς ἐπιτήδειος ἐναποκυῆσαι καὶ ἐκθρέψαι τὰ ἔκγονα. Ἐπειδὰν δὲ τὸ σπουδαζόμενον ἀρκούντως ἐκπληρωθῇ, πάλιν πανδημεὶ πάντες ὑποστρέφουσιν οἴκαδε. Καὶ τίς ὁ λόγος, ἀκούσωμεν παρὰ τῶν σιωπώντων. Ἐπιπόλαιος, φασὶν, ἡ βορεινὴ θάλασσα, καὶ ὑπτία προκειμένη τῶν ἀνέμων ταῖς βίαις, ὀλίγας ἀκτὰς καὶ ὑποδρομὰς ἔχουσα. Διὸ καὶ ἐκ πυθμένος οἱ ἄνεμοι ῥᾳδίως αὐτὴν ἀναστρέφουσιν, ὡς καὶ τὴν βυθίαν ψάμμον τοῖς κύμασιν ἀναμίγνυσθαι. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ψυχρὰ, χειμῶνος ὥρᾳ, ὑπὸ πολλῶν καὶ μεγάλων ποταμῶν πληρουμένη. Διὰ τοῦτο ἐφ' ὅσον μέτριον ἀπολαύσαντες αὐτῆς ἐν τῷ θέρει, πάλιν χειμῶνος ἐπὶ τὴν ἐν τῷ βυθῷ ἀλέαν καὶ τὰ προσήλια τῶν χωρίων ἐπείγονται, καὶ φυγόντες τὸ δυσήνεμον τῶν ἀρκτῴων, τοῖς ἐπ' ἔλαττον τινασσομένοις κόλποις ἐγκαθορμίζονται. 7.5 Εἶδον ταῦτα ἐγὼ, καὶ τὴν ἐν πᾶσι τοῦ Θεοῦ σοφίαν ἐθαύμασα. Εἰ τὰ ἄλογα ἐπινοητικὰ καὶ φυλακτικὰ τῆς ἰδίας αὐτῶν σωτηρίας, καὶ οἶδε τὸ αἱρετὸν αὐτῷ καὶ τὸ φευκτὸν ὁ ἰχθὺς, τί ἐροῦμεν ἡμεῖς οἱ λόγῳ τετιμημένοι, καὶ νόμῳ πεπαιδευμένοι, ἐπαγγελίαις προτραπέντες, Πνεύματι σοφισθέντες, εἶτα τῶν ἰχθύων ἀλογώτερον τὰ καθ' ἑαυτοὺς διατιθέμενοι; Εἴπερ οἱ μὲν ἴσασι τοῦ μέλλοντός τινα ποιεῖσθαι πρόνοιαν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐκ τῆς πρὸς τὸ μέλλον ἀνελπιστίας δι' ἡδονῆς βοσκηματώδους τὴν ζωὴν ἀναλίσκομεν. Ἰχθὺς τοσαῦτα διαμείβει πελάγη ὑπὲρ τοῦ εὕρασθαί τινα ὠφέλειαν· τί ἐρεῖς σὺ ὁ τῇ ἀργίᾳ συζῶν; Ἀργία δὲ, κακουργίας ἀρχή. Μηδεὶς ἄγνοιαν προφασιζέσθω. Φυσικὸς λόγος οἰκείωσιν ἡμῖν τοῦ καλοῦ, καὶ ἀλλοτρίωσιν ἀπὸ τῶν βλαβερῶν ὑποδεικνὺς ἐγκατέσπαρται. Οὐκ ἀφίσταμαι τῶν θαλασσίων ὑποδειγμάτων, ἐπειδὴ ταῦτα ἡμῖν πρόκειται εἰς ἐξέτασιν. Ἤκουσα ἐγὼ τῶν παραλίων τινὸς, ὅτι ὁ θαλάσσιος ἐχῖνος, τὸ μικρὸν παντελῶς καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητον ζῷον, διδάσκαλος πολλάκις γαλήνης καὶ κλύδωνος τοῖς πλέουσι γίνεται. Ὃς ὅταν προΐδῃ ταραχὴν ἐξ ἀνέμων, ψηφῖδά τινα ὑπελθὼν γενναίαν, ἐπ' αὐτῆς, ὥσπερ ἐπ' ἀγκύρας, βεβαίως σαλεύει, κατεχόμενος τῷ βάρει πρὸς τὸ μὴ ῥᾳδίως τοῖς κύμασιν ὑποσύρεσθαι. Τοῦτο ὅταν ἴδωσιν οἱ ναυτικοὶ τὸ σημεῖον, ἴσασι τὴν προσδοκωμένην βιαίαν κίνησιν τῶν ἀνέμων. Οὐδεὶς ἀστρολόγος, οὐδεὶς Χαλδαῖος, ταῖς ἐπιτο λαῖς τῶν ἄστρων τὰς τῶν ἀέρων ταραχὰς τεκμαιρόμενος, ταῦτα τὸν ἐχῖνον ἐδίδαξεν, ἀλλ' ὁ θαλάσσης καὶ ἀνέμων Κύριος καὶ τῷ μικρῷ ζῴῳ τῆς μεγάλης ἑαυτοῦ σοφίας ἐναργὲς ἴχνος ἐνέθηκεν. Οὐδὲν ἀπρονόητον, οὐδὲν ἠμελημένον παρὰ Θεοῦ. Πάντα σκοπεύει ὁ ἀκοίμητος ὀφθαλμός. Πᾶσι πάρεστιν, ἐκπορίζων ἑκάστῳ τὴν σωτηρίαν. Εἰ ἐχῖνον ἔξω τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἐπισκοπῆς ὁ Θεὸς οὐκ ἀφῆκε, τὰ σὰ οὐκ ἐπισκοπεῖ; Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, κἂν ὑπερόριοι ἀλλήλοις πρὸς κοινωνίαν γάμου συνέλθητε. Ὁ τῆς φύσεως δεσμὸς, ὁ διὰ τῆς εὐλογίας ζυγὸς, ἕνωσις ἔστω τῶν διεστώτων.
thought_title: Fish and sea urchin teach providence and marital fidelity
orientation: Basil is preaching on the fifth day's water creatures, drawing moral lessons from fish migrations and the sea urchin's storm-sensing behavior.
pass_a_gloss: They do not have their own reason, but they have the law of nature strongly implanted, and it points out what must be done. Let us go, they say, to the northern sea. For that water is sweeter than the rest of the sea, because the sun, spending only a little time upon it, does not draw out all its drinkable water through its ray. And sea creatures rejoice in sweet waters; whence also they often swim up into rivers, and are carried far from the sea. From this the Black Sea is more preferred by them than the other gulfs, as being suitable for hatching and rearing their offspring. But when the desired thing has been sufficiently fulfilled, again all together in a body they all return home. And what is the reason, let us hear from those who are silent. The northern sea, they say, is shallow, and lying flat and exposed to the forces of the winds, having few shores and refuges. Therefore also from the bottom the winds easily turn it over, so that even the deep sand is mixed with the waves. But it is also cold, in the winter season, being filled by many and great rivers. For this reason, after enjoying it moderately in the summer, again in winter they hasten to the warmth in the deep and the sun-facing places of the regions, and fleeing the storminess of the northern parts, they anchor in the gulfs that are shaken less. 7.5 I have seen these things, and I marveled at the wisdom of God in all things. If irrational creatures are inventive and protective of their own safety, and the fish knows what is to be chosen by it and what is to be avoided, what shall we say, we who have been honored with reason, and instructed by law, urged on by promises, made wise by the Spirit, and then we arrange our own affairs more irrationally than the fish? If indeed they know how to make some provision for the future, but we, from hopelessness toward the future, through brutish pleasure waste our life away. A fish crosses so many seas for the sake of finding some benefit; what will you say, you who live with idleness? And idleness is the beginning of wickedness. Let no one plead ignorance as an excuse. A natural reason has been sown in us, pointing out the affinity with the good and the estrangement from harmful things. I do not depart from the examples of sea creatures, since these are set before us for examination. I heard from one of the coastal people that the sea urchin, the altogether small and contemptible animal, often becomes a teacher of calm and of storm to sailors. Which, whenever it foresees disturbance from winds, going under some sizable pebble, upon it, as upon an anchor, it rides securely, held down by the weight so as not to be easily dragged under by the waves. Whenever the sailors see this sign, they know the expected violent movement of the winds. No astrologer, no Chaldean, inferring the disturbances of the airs from the risings of the stars, taught these things to the urchin, but the Lord of sea and winds also placed in the small animal a clear trace of his great wisdom. Nothing is unprovided for, nothing neglected by God. The sleepless eye watches all things. He is present to all, furnishing to each its safety. If God did not leave the urchin outside his own oversight, does he not oversee your affairs? Husbands, love your wives, even if you have come together with one another from foreign lands for the communion of marriage. Let the bond of nature, the yoke through the blessing, be a union of those who are separated.

choices.term: τὸν τῆς φύσεως νόμον ἰσχυρῶς ἐνιδρυμένον
choices.english: the law of nature strongly implanted
choices.why: Keeps the passive participle force of 'implanted' and the adverb 'strongly' to show the law is fixed within creatures by God, not self-generated
rejected: the law of nature firmly established

choices.english: pointing out what must be done
choices.why: Preserves the verbal adjective 'what must be done' and the present participle 'pointing out' as an ongoing function of the natural law

choices.english: all together in a body they all return home
choices.why: Renders the rare adverb 'πανδημεί' with its collective force and keeps the redundancy with 'πάντες' as emphatic in the source
rejected: they all return home en masse

choices.term: ὑπτία προκειμένη τῶν ἀνέμων ταῖς βίαις
choices.english: lying flat and exposed to the forces of the winds
choices.why: Keeps the physical image of 'ὑπτία' (supine, flat) and the dative of exposure 'to the forces of the winds'
rejected: lying open to the violence of the winds
spread out before the winds' force

choices.term: ἐπινοητικὰ καὶ φυλακτικὰ τῆς ἰδίας αὐτῶν σωτηρίας
choices.english: inventive and protective of their own safety
choices.why: Renders both adjectives with their full force: 'inventive' for devising means and 'protective' for guarding their safety
rejected: resourceful and careful of their own preservation
clever and watchful for their own safety

choices.why: Captures the pejorative force of the adjective derived from 'βοσκήμα' (grazing animal), implying cattle-like, pleasure-driven living

pass_b_english: They have no reason of their own, but they have the law of nature strongly implanted in them, pointing out what must be done. "Let us go," they say, "to the northern sea." For its water is sweeter than the rest of the sea, because the sun spends only a little time upon it and does not draw out all its drinkable quality through its rays. Sea creatures also delight in sweet water; that is why they often swim up into rivers and travel far from the sea. For this reason the Black Sea is more prized by them than the other gulfs, as a place suited for hatching and rearing their young. But when the object of their eagerness has been sufficiently accomplished, all together in a body they all return home again. And what is the reason? Let us hear it from those who are silent. "The northern sea," they say, "is shallow, and lying flat and exposed to the forces of the winds, it has few shores and places of refuge. Therefore the winds easily turn it over from its very depths, so that even the sand from the bottom is mixed with the waves. It is also cold in the winter season, filled by many great rivers." For this reason, after enjoying it moderately in the summer, in winter they hasten again to the warmth in the deep and the sun-facing regions, and fleeing the storminess of the northern waters, they anchor in the gulfs that are less shaken.

I have seen these things myself, and I marveled at the wisdom of God in all things. If irrational creatures are inventive and protective of their own safety, and the fish knows what is to be chosen and what is to be avoided, what shall we say—we who have been honored with reason, instructed by law, urged on by promises, made wise by the Spirit—if we then manage our own affairs more irrationally than the fish? For they know how to exercise some forethought for the future, while we, through hopelessness about what is to come, consume our lives in a beast-like way. A fish crosses such vast seas to find some benefit. What will you say, you who live with idleness? Idleness is the beginning of wickedness. Let no one plead ignorance. A natural reason has been sown within us, showing us our kinship with the good and our alienation from harmful things.

I do not depart from the examples of the sea, since these are set before us for examination. I have heard from one of the coastal people that the sea urchin, that tiny and utterly contemptible creature, often becomes a teacher of calm and of storm to sailors. Whenever it foresees a disturbance from the winds, it gets under a sizable pebble and rides securely upon it as upon an anchor, held by the weight so that it is not easily dragged away by the waves. When sailors see this sign, they know that a violent movement of the winds is to be expected. No astrologer, no Chaldean, who infers disturbances of the air from the risings of the stars, taught these things to the urchin; rather, the Lord of the sea and the winds placed in this small creature a clear trace of his great wisdom. Nothing is without providence, nothing is neglected by God. The unsleeping eye watches over all things. He is present to all, providing safety for each one. If God did not leave the urchin outside his own care, does he not watch over your affairs?

Husbands, love your wives, even if you have come together from distant lands for the communion of marriage. Let the bond of nature, the yoke given through blessing, be the union of those who were separated.

problems.why: 'ἀλέαν' means warmth/heat, but 'ἐν τῷ βυθῷ' specifies 'in the deep' as location; fish flee TO deep warmth, not 'warmth of the deep' as abstract.
problems.fix: to the warmth in the deep

problems.quote: all together in a body they all return home
problems.why: Source says 'again' (πάλιν) which is dropped; 'all together in a body' renders πανδημεὶ but 'πάλιν' meaning 'back/again' is missing.
problems.fix: all together in a body they all return home again
problems.ruling: πάλιν ('again/back') is omitted; 'all together in a body they all return home' loses the 'again' sense, changing the temporal logic of the migration cycle.

edits.old: all together in a body they all return home
edits.new: all together in a body they all return home again

fixed: Changed 'the warmth of the deep' to 'the warmth in the deep' to reflect the source 'τὴν ἐν τῷ βυθῷ ἀλέαν', where 'ἐν τῷ βυθῷ' specifies location.
Added 'again' to 'all together in a body they all return home' to restore the source's 'πάλιν'.

problems.quote: what is akin to the good and what is alien to harmful things
problems.source_quote: οἰκείωσιν ἡμῖν τοῦ καλοῦ, καὶ ἀλλοτρίωσιν ἀπὸ τῶν βλαβερῶν
problems.why: Source says 'making the good our own and alienating us from harmful things'; English reverses the alienation direction.
problems.fix: our kinship with the good and our alienation from harmful things
problems.ruling: ἀλλοτρίωσιν ἀπὸ τῶν βλαβερῶν = 'alienation FROM harmful things,' not 'alien TO harmful things'; direction reversed.

problems.why: Basil quotes no verse; Ephesians 5:25 is added by translator.
problems.ruling: Source has no scripture reference; translator adds '(Ephesians 5:25)' not in Greek text.

edits.new: our kinship with the good and our alienation from harmful things

edits.new: Husbands, love your wives, even if

fixed: mistranslation: source 'οἰκείωσιν ἡμῖν τοῦ καλοῦ, καὶ ἀλλοτρίωσιν ἀπὸ τῶν βλαβερῶν' means 'making the good our own and alienating us from harmful things'; English reversed the alienation direction. Fixed.
wrong_scripture: source 'Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας' is Basil's own exhortation, not a quotation of Ephesians 5:25. Removed the added citation.

problems.why: βυθίαν means 'of the deep sea bottom,' but context shows this is about shallowness—winds churn up bottom sand because sea is shallow.
βοσκηματώδους modifies 'life,' not 'pleasure'; we consume our life in beast-like manner, not 'brutish pleasure.'
problems.fix: consume our lives in a beast-like way
problems.ruling: βοσκηματώδους modifies ζωὴν not ἡδονῆς; 'brutish pleasure' wrongly attaches beast-like to pleasure not life.

edits.old: waste our lives in brutish pleasure
edits.new: consume our lives in a beast-like way

fixed: Changed 'the sand of the deep' to 'the sand from the bottom' because βυθίαν ψάμμον refers to the sand at the sea bottom, and the context emphasizes the shallowness allowing winds to churn it up.

Changed 'waste our lives in brutish pleasure' to 'consume our lives in a beast-like way' because βοσκηματώδους modifies 'life' (τὴν ζωὴν), not 'pleasure'; the Greek says we consume our life in a beast-like manner.

last_rejected.quote: few shores and places of refuge
last_rejected.why: ὑποδρομάς means 'inlets' or 'creeks,' not 'places of refuge.'
last_rejected.ruling: ὑποδρομάς (under-runnings) can mean 'inlets, creeks'; 'places of refuge' is a reasonable extension.

last_rejected.why: ἀλέαν means 'warmth/heat,' but 'in the deep' is wrong; βυθῷ here likely refers to deep water warmth.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐν τῷ βυθῷ literally means 'in the deep'; warmth located in the deep is accurate.

last_rejected.why: συζῶν means 'living in union with,' 'yoked to,' stronger than 'live with.'
last_rejected.fix: you who are yoked to idleness
last_rejected.ruling: συζῶν with dative means 'live with'; 'live with idleness' captures the sense adequately.

last_rejected.why: οἰκείωσιν means 'familiarization/affinity,' not 'kinship'; it's about relationship, not family tie.
last_rejected.ruling: οἰκείωσιν means 'kinship, affinity, familiarization'; 'kinship' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: γενναίαν means 'sturdy/substantial,' not 'sizable'; emphasizes strength, not size.
last_rejected.ruling: γενναίαν can mean 'noble, stout, sizable'; 'sizable' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: who infers disturbances of the air from the risings of the stars

last_rejected.why: ἐπιτολαῖς means 'risings' technically, but 'risings of the stars' is misleading; better 'positions' or 'heliacal risings.'
last_rejected.fix: who infers disturbances of the air from the stars' positions
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπιτολαῖς means 'risings'; 'risings of the stars' is the standard meaning, not misleading.

last_rejected.why: ἐπισκοπῆς means 'oversight/watch,' but 'care' weakens it; 'outside his oversight' or 'beyond his watch.'
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπισκοπῆς means 'oversight, care, visitation'; 'care' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: even if you have come together from distant lands
last_rejected.source_quote: κἂν ὑπερόριοι ἀλλήλοις πρὸς κοινωνίαν γάμου συνέλθητε
last_rejected.why: ὑπερόριοι means 'from different countries/foreign,' but 'distant lands' is loose; 'foreign to one another' is closer.
last_rejected.fix: even if you are foreign to one another
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπερόριοι means 'from beyond borders'; 'from distant lands' is a reasonable rendering.

last_rejected.quote: Let the bond of nature, the yoke given through blessing, be the union of those who were separated.
last_rejected.source_quote: Ὁ τῆς φύσεως δεσμὸς, ὁ διὰ τῆς εὐλογίας ζυγός, ἕνωσις ἔστω τῶν διεστώτων.
last_rejected.why: Missing 'let...be' imperative force; also 'given through blessing' obscures that εὐλογίας is 'the blessing' (of marriage).
last_rejected.fix: Let the bond of nature, the yoke of blessing, be the union of those who were separated.
last_rejected.ruling: ἔστω is rendered 'Let...be'; 'given through blessing' captures διὰ τῆς εὐλογίας adequately.
